newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China extends clampdown against diesel smuggling.
newsitem.headline: China extends clampdown against diesel smuggling.

text.p: China is intensifying its crackdown on diesel smuggling to other provinces after the illicit trade shifted from the traditional hot spots in southern Guangdong, Chinese officials and traders said on Tuesday.

The anti-smuggling drive is now directed at Fujian, Hainan and Guanxi provinces after intensive checks along the Guangdong coastline, several months before Hong Kong's handover to Chinese rule on July 1, have dampened smuggling there.

"We have received a lot of reports about the serious situation recently, especially in Fujian and Hainan... we are holding meetings to work out measures to solve the problem," said an official with China's State Planning Commission.
"While the crackdown may have dampened the illicit trade in Guangdong, smugglers were smart enought to move elsewhere," one Chinese trader said.
Apart from routine patrol checks along the southeastern coast to nab smugglers, authorities will intensify crackdown in Guangdong's neighbouring provinces, the official said.

"In the past Guangdong was the most serious smuggling area, but now the smuggling moved up to Fujian and down to Hainan after we conducted intensive checks in Guangdong in past few months," the official said from Beijing.
Officials from the State Planning Commission were also meeting in Beijing to study how to boost domestic retail diesel prices but he declined to give further details, he said.
Diesel imports this year have surged to 2.4 million tonnes in the first four months, a 77 percent jump from a year ago.
"Of the diesel China imported so far this year, at least 700,000 tonnes are still unsold," said a source with state China National Petrochemicals Imports and Export Corp (Sinochem).
The rise in imports amid falling international prices has led to a fall in retail prices. Smuggling has added to domestic supplies forcing retail prices to slip, the official added.
On the other hand, the illicit trade was prompted by high wholesale diesel prices from China's refineries, making it profitable to smuggle cargoes amid lower international prices.
Current ex-refinery diesel price is 2,190 yuan a tonne, compared with international prices with cargoes being sold at over $160 a tonne, on a cost-and-freight southern China basis.
This could yield a profit of 500-800 yuan a tonne ($60-$100) if the cargoes were smuggled into China, traders said.
Coastal Guangdong has been nortorious for diesel smuggling from Hong Kong, where many trading firms used boats to transport diesel into China without paying customs duties and tax.
Hong Kong officially exports about 200,000 tonnes of diesel to China each month but some traders said almost the same amount were being smuggled monthly.
"The situation in Guangdong has improved a lot this year, thanks to security concerns before the handover," said a trader with a Chinese state oil company in Singapore.

Chinese state media reported that about one million tonnes of diesel have been smuggled into China so far this year. But traders said the actual amount is much higher, with one seeing as much as 1.5 million tonnes in the first half of 1997.
China produced 43 million tonnes of diesel in 1996 and imported 4.6 million tonnes, according to official figures.

Chinese media has reported that about 150,000 tonnes of diesel have been smuggled through eastern coastal Zhejiang province alone in the last three months and other coastal provinces were also seeing the illicit trade.

"Smuggling from Hong Kong may quiet down if the Chinese crackdown gets serious, but if it's not persistent, which is likely, the smuggling will continue soon after the handover because it's so profitable," said one trader in Singapore.
--Singapore Newsroom (65-870-3571)
